title: What happens when AI splits up your friend group?
excerpt: Between ethical debates and Claude-generated texts, AI use is causing tension in friend groups. Is there a way forward?
content_html:
In San Francisco, Julie Krafchick, co-host of “ The Psychology of Relationships,” was working on podcast episodes and researching how people connect, but still keeping up with friends in media and tech. In some friend circles, you were falling behind if you weren’t using AI models to “10x” your life and work. In others, dinner talk consisted of debates over whether The New York Times or Granta had published AI-generated work. 

Krafchick was torn. On one hand, she could see AI’s potential; she’d had a career in tech. But in both circles, she found herself deliberating how and when to talk about AI. In one exchange, a friend told her how her latest Claude project was something she had “put her heart and soul” into. 

But Krafchick didn’t necessarily view AI that way. “Personally, I want to do [creative] work,” she told Big Think. “I want to get my hands wet. So there can be a divide…when it almost feels like your friend is taking a shortcut.” Part of her felt she had worked for years to master the craft, only to have someone else “put in a prompt.” 

Still, it felt a bit dramatic to question her friend’s choice. “I do feel like this is something that…does feel like an off-limits topic,” she added. “You wonder: Why am I getting upset about AI and someone using it?” 

A new taboo

If you’ve ever felt like AI is a fraught topic, you’re not alone. You likely have at least one connection who, by virtue of their age, occupation, or feelings about the tech industry, disagrees strongly with your stance on artificial intelligence. Although AI use continues to rise, a Bentley-Gallup survey from July found that, compared with recent years, more Americans now say AI causes more harm than good, especially young adults, who are roughly split on the issue. 

Fundamentally, these friendship disagreements make sense. Like finance, politics, or sex, AI is one of those topics that holds a multitude of sensitive spots underneath. Did you study for a decade in a field threatened by AI? Are you jealous of your friend who’s set to make millions? Do you hate its use of environmental resources? Are you heavily invested in AI stocks? Often, a theoretical “AI” conversation rapidly triggers personal, practical feelings about its impact. 

Complicating things, friends may cover up their use of AI, depending on the degree to which they think others will accept it. As Sarah Newman, Director of Art & Education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, discovered when she started collecting anonymous confessions from strangers, more people than you may think have “guilty AI secrets,” or ways in which they use AI they don’t feel comfortable fully admitting in public. Should you ask your friend if they generated your wedding speech? What happens if you receive an AI-written apology text? And what if you’re ethically opposed to the AI industry and your friend goes to work at Anthropic?

Most of the time, friends stay quiet. Even though there are plenty of reasons why AI use is such a high-tension topic — environmental ethics, copyright, and AI layoffs, to name a few — “it almost feels weird,” Krafchick explained, “to confront it.” 

Overrelying on AI

Thanks to her podcast, Krafchick is on the front lines of AI-related friendship debates. For one, AI-mediated advice is making it hard to disagree without behind-the-scenes influence. Friends turn to chatbots to talk through conflicts in friend groups, or even forward AI transcript logs to prove their point. “You’ve probably seen that before with friend groups,” she told Big Think. “People…will just copy and paste.” It’s that sense of: “Claude told me this, so it must be right.” 

As Yael Schonbrun, a clinical psychologist and the author of Why Don’t You Understand Me? The Surprising Science Behind Connecting in a World of Missed Signals, explained that heavy AI use between friends can ultimately chip away at both authenticity and trust. When we use LLMs to edit and “make what we say and think kind of refined,” she pointed out, we risk losing the vulnerability that makes a friendship work. 

Other times, friends may turn to AI to smooth over a conflict, especially if a situation is tense and they don’t know what to say. Asking a friend whether they used AI to craft a message is uncomfortable, but so is not knowing. “When you get a text that almost feels overly polished,” Krafchick told Big Think, “you’re like, ‘Did AI write this or did you write this?’” 

Not everyone, of course, wants to automate friendship. “Some of the best parts of friendship are the wildly inefficient/random/silly texts,” Meagan Phelan, a communications director at Science Journals & Publishing, wrote in response to the launch of AI-integrated text messages. She chalked the value of thoughtful check-ins up to intention, noting that taking away those tiny moments is “a very efficient way to become worse at being a friend.” 

Over time, consistently using AI to communicate can alienate and divide friend groups, especially if one or more people feel like their friends aren’t putting in personal effort. “There’s a larger conversation we need to have,” Schonbrun said, “about the way that AI fits into our relationships.” 

But friendship breakups can’t be the only way forward. So what might it take to get past our initial discomfort and have better conversations? 

A more constructive debate 

Part of the answer seems to be interrogating our own assumptions, taking time to articulate our viewpoints, and leading with curiosity rather than judgment. 

While an AI model can help us understand a friend’s point of view or express our feelings less confrontationally, Krafchick pointed out, from a friendship perspective, it’s typically best to avoid letting AI provide a word-for-word script. If “one friend goes to AI…and then they figure out what to say to the second because AI has given them [the exact words],” she elaborated, that’s when the debate starts to feel “disingenuous.” 

Instead, Schonbrun and Krafchick suggest we approach the conversation with our own words, and get curious. If you disagree, why does your friend feel that way? Are there any potential areas of overlap? What have they read or watched that they think best explains their reasoning behind a take? What’s been their personal experience? And finally — if you ever want to talk about it in a social context — what are their boundaries and how would they like to talk about it? 

In Krafchick’s friend group, the choice isn’t “AI or no AI” so much as it is chatting with the friends she’s with about ideas that catch their interest. Sometimes that’s AI; sometimes it’s not. If she’s at Sunday brunch, she might be fascinated by conversations about how AI might shape relationships moving forward, but less so by talk centered on building agents. “It’s finding what topic within AI makes sense for you,” she added.

While AI models are increasingly used as both advisor and friend, Schonbrun explained, they don’t replace the intimacy of a real friendship. If anything, they create a false expectation of how friendships — the kind that challenge and inspire us — are supposed to work. “We need to have a stake in the game in order for relationships to have depth,” she told Big Think. “For them to grow, [and] for us to be able to grow along with them.”
